title: Specialized investments, contract length and optimal procurement
summary: What specialized investments are, their four types, why they raise transaction costs, how they and contracting complexity change optimal contract length, and the decision tree for choosing a procurement method.

chunks.heading: What specialized investments are
chunks.explanation_md:
Imagine a supplier who builds a factory **right next to** your plant, or buys a machine that only makes **your** part. If you walk away, that investment is almost useless.

That is a **specialized investment**: it allows the two parties to exchange but has **little or no value outside the relationship**.

Because one side is now locked in, these investments **raise transaction costs**: **costly bargaining**, **underinvestment** (nobody wants to be the one stuck) and **opportunism and the hold-up problem**.

key_terms.meaning: An investment that allows two parties to exchange but has little or no value outside the exchange relationship

chunks.exam_line: Four types: site specificity, physical-asset specificity, dedicated assets, human capital. They cause costly bargaining, underinvestment and hold-up.

chunks.exam_answer_md: **Specialized investments** are investments made to allow two parties to exchange but which have little or no value outside the exchange relationship. Types: site specificity, physical-asset specificity, dedicated assets, human capital. They lead to higher transaction costs through costly bargaining, underinvestment, and opportunism and the hold-up problem.

chunks.heading: Contract length: marginal benefit meets marginal cost
chunks.explanation_md:
How long should a contract be? Where the **marginal benefit** of one more year equals its **marginal cost**.

- A **longer** contract protects specialized investments from hold-up, so when specialized investments matter more, the **MB curve shifts out** and the contract gets **longer**.
- A **longer** contract is harder to write when the future is complicated, so a **more complex contracting environment** shifts **MC up** and the contract gets **shorter**. A **simpler** environment does the opposite.
chunks.exam_line: More specialized investment: longer contracts. More complex contracting environment: shorter contracts.

chunks.memory_trick: **Locked in? Lock it longer. Complicated? Keep it short.**
chunks.exam_answer_md:
The optimal contract length is where the marginal benefit (MB) of extending the contract equals its marginal cost (MC).

- **Greater need for specialized investments** raises MB (MB0 to MB1): **longer contract** (L0 to L1). Example: a supplier building a plant next to the buyer wants a long contract.
- **More complex contracting environment** raises MC (MC0 to MC2): **shorter contract** (L0 to L2).
- **Less complex environment** lowers MC (MC0 to MC1): **longer contract**.

(Draw the two graphs with contract length on the x-axis.)

chunks.heading: Choosing the method: the decision tree
chunks.explanation_md:
Follow the tree from the top.

- If there are **no substantial specialized investments**, nobody can be held up, so just use the **spot market**.
- If there **are**, you need protection. If writing a contract is **not** too complex compared with the cost of integrating, use a **contract**.
- If it **is** too complex, **make the input yourself** (vertical integration).
chunks.exam_line: No big specialized investment: spot. Big specialized investment, simple contracting: contract. Big specialized investment, complex contracting: vertical integration.

chunks.big_idea: Ask two questions: are the specialized investments big, and is a contract too hard to write? The answers pick spot, contract or integration.

nodes.label: Substantial specialized investments relative to contracting costs?
Complex contracting environment relative to costs of integration?

watch_out: Spot exchange is the answer only when specialized investments are **not** substantial.
chunks.exam_answer_md: Optimal input procurement: if specialized investments are not substantial relative to contracting costs, use **spot exchange**. If they are, and the contracting environment is not complex relative to the costs of integration, use a **contract**; if it is complex, use **vertical integration**. The optimal method depends on the nature of transaction costs and the specialized nature of the inputs.
